three-sisters-agriculture.name: Three Sisters
three-sisters-agriculture.summary: A companion-planting method combining maize, beans and squash, in which each crop supports the others, developed by Indigenous peoples of the Americas.

nixtamalization.name: Nixtamalization
nixtamalization.summary: A process of soaking and cooking maize in an alkaline solution such as limewater, which improves its nutrition and flavor and makes it possible to form dough (masa).

metate.name: Metate
metate.summary: A ground stone tool, a type of quern, traditionally used in Mesoamerica—mainly by women—to grind nixtamalized maize and other foods such as tortillas.

comal-cookware.name: Comal
comal-cookware.summary: A smooth, flat griddle used across Mexico and Central America to cook tortillas, toast spices and sear meat, often handed down through generations.

motagua-river.name: Motagua River
motagua-river.summary: A 486-km river in Guatemala whose valley holds jadeite deposits long used by Indigenous Mesoamerican peoples.

phaseolus-vulgaris.name: Phaseolus vulgaris
phaseolus-vulgaris.summary: The common bean, a plant native to the Americas domesticated about 8,000 years ago and today the most consumed bean species in the world.

teotihuacan.name: Teotihuacan
teotihuacan.summary: An ancient Mesoamerican city near modern Mexico City, home to the Pyramid of the Sun and Pyramid of the Moon, likely the largest city in the Americas around 1 to 500 CE with up to 100,000 people.

pyramid-of-the-sun.name: Pyramid of the Sun
pyramid-of-the-sun.summary: The largest building at Teotihuacan, Mexico, and one of the largest in Mesoamerica, believed to have been built around 200 AD along the Avenue of the Dead.

pyramid-of-the-moon.name: Pyramid of the Moon
pyramid-of-the-moon.summary: The second-largest pyramid at Teotihuacan, Mexico, built in phases between about 100 and 450 CE over an older structure and used for ceremonies and ritual sacrifices honoring the Great Goddess.

temple-of-the-feathered-serpent-teotihua.name: Temple of the Feathered Serpent
temple-of-the-feathered-serpent-teotihua.summary: The third-largest pyramid at Teotihuacan in central Mexico, dated to around 150-200 CE, known for feathered-serpent carvings and more than a hundred sacrificial burials found beneath it.
temple-of-the-feathered-serpent-teotihua.source_title: Temple of the Feathered Serpent, Teotihuacan

jaina-island.name: Jaina Island
jaina-island.summary: Small artificial limestone island off Mexico's Yucatán coast that served as an elite Maya burial site, known for its finely detailed ceramic figurines.

tikal.name: Tikal
tikal.summary: A ruined ancient Maya city in Guatemala's rainforest that was capital of one of the most powerful Maya kingdoms, peaking roughly between 200 and 900 CE.

calakmul.name: Calakmul
calakmul.summary: A major Maya city in Mexico's Petén Basin, seat of the powerful 'Snake Kingdom' during the Classic period, with an estimated population of 50,000.

motul-de-san-jos.name: Motul de San José
motul-de-san-jos.summary: Ancient Maya city near Lake Petén Itzá in Guatemala, an important Late Classic political center that shifted allegiance between Tikal and Calakmul.

north-acropolis-tikal.name: North Acropolis
north-acropolis-tikal.summary: Complex at the Maya city of Tikal that served as a royal necropolis and centre of funerary activity for over 1,300 years, holding the tombs of several named Tikal kings.

maya-hero-twins.name: Hero Twins
maya-hero-twins.summary: The central figures of the Popol Vuh myth, Hunahpu and Xbalanque, often portrayed as complementary forces in Classic Maya art and linked to royal dynastic claims of divine ancestry.

el-taj-n.name: El Tajín
el-taj-n.summary: A pre-Columbian archaeological site in Veracruz, Mexico, one of the largest Classic-era Mesoamerican cities, flourishing from 600 to 1200 CE and known for its Pyramid of the Niches.

pulque.name: Pulque
pulque.summary: A milky, sour, fermented alcoholic drink made from agave sap, traditional in central Mexico for millennia; once sacred and restricted, it became widely popular after the Spanish conquest, peaking in the late 19th century.

pet-n-basin.name: Petén
pet-n-basin.summary: A subregion of the Maya Lowlands in northern Guatemala where major Maya centers such as Tikal and Calakmul flourished.

macuahuitl.name: Macuahuitl
macuahuitl.summary: A Mesoamerican sword lined with obsidian blades sharper than steel razors, used as a standard close-combat weapon since at least the first millennium CE by the Aztec, Maya and other civilizations.

mixtec.name: Mixtec
mixtec.summary: Indigenous Mesoamerican peoples of Oaxaca, Puebla and Guerrero, Mexico, whose civilization lasted from about 1500 BCE until the Spanish conquest in 1523.

toltec.name: Toltec
toltec.summary: A pre-Columbian Mesoamerican culture centered at Tula, Mexico, that reached prominence from about 950 to 1150 AD and was regarded by the later Aztecs as their cultural predecessor.

nahuan-languages.name: Nahuan (Aztecan) languages
nahuan-languages.summary: A branch of the Uto-Aztecan language family, including Nahuatl, defined by a sound change turning an original *t into /tɬ/; today spoken by about 1.7 million Nahua people.

valley-of-mexico.name: Valley of Mexico
valley-of-mexico.summary: A large basin in the highlands of central Mexico that was home to pre-Columbian civilizations including Teotihuacan and the Aztec Empire, and now contains Mexico City.

mesoamerican-postclassic-period.name: Postclassic period
mesoamerican-postclassic-period.summary: The final period of independent Mesoamerican civilization, roughly 900 to 1521 CE, marked by urbanization, commerce and migrations, ending with Spanish colonization.

monte-alb-n.name: Monte Albán
monte-alb-n.summary: An ancient hilltop city in Oaxaca, Mexico, founded around 500 BCE, that served as the main political and economic center of the Zapotec civilization for nearly a thousand years.

oaxaca.name: Oaxaca
oaxaca.summary: One of Mexico's 31 states, in the south of the country, known for its Indigenous peoples, especially the Zapotecs and Mixtecs, and archaeological sites such as Monte Albán.

sierra-de-las-navajas.name: Sierra de las Navajas
sierra-de-las-navajas.summary: A mountain range in central Mexico and one of the most important obsidian sources in Mesoamerica, its green obsidian used for over 3,000 years by societies including Teotihuacan and Tenochtitlan.

nahuatl.name: Nahuatl
nahuatl.summary: A language of the Uto-Aztecan family spoken in central Mexico since at least the 7th century CE, once the prestige language of the Aztec Empire.

olmecs.name: Olmecs
olmecs.summary: An early Mesoamerican civilization that flourished roughly 1200 to 400 BC in what is now Veracruz and Tabasco, known for colossal stone heads and considered one of the cradles of civilization.

zapotec-civilization.name: Zapotec civilization
zapotec-civilization.summary: A pre-Columbian civilization of Mexico's Valley of Oaxaca, flourishing from about 700 BC to 1521 CE, whose city Monte Albán was one of Mesoamerica's first major urban centers.

amate.name: Amate
amate.summary: A type of bark paper made in Mexico since precontact times, used for Mayan and Aztec codices and records, whose production survived the Spanish conquest in remote mountain villages.

rebus.name: Rebus
rebus.summary: A puzzle device combining pictures and letters to represent words by their sound, historically a favored form of heraldic expression used to encode surnames in the Middle Ages.

oaxaca-valley.name: Oaxaca Valley
oaxaca-valley.summary: A valley within the modern Mexican state of Oaxaca that was home to the Zapotec civilization and later Mixtec culture, and holds major sites such as Monte Albán and Mitla.

tula-mesoamerican-site.name: Tula
tula-mesoamerican-site.summary: An archaeological site in central Mexico that became the capital of the Toltec Empire, flourishing between the decline of Teotihuacan and the rise of Tenochtitlan before falling around 1150.

tenochtitlan.name: Tenochtitlan
tenochtitlan.summary: The Aztec capital built on an island in Lake Texcoco, founded around 1325, that grew into the largest city in the pre-Columbian Americas before its capture in 1521.

classical-nahuatl.name: Classical Nahuatl
classical-nahuatl.summary: The form of Nahuatl spoken as a lingua franca in central Mexico at the time of the 16th-century Spanish conquest, later evolving into modern Nahuan languages.

totonac.name: Totonac
totonac.summary: Indigenous people of Mexico, possible builders of the pre-Columbian city of El Tajín, who were the world's main vanilla producers until the mid-19th century.

mixe-zoque-languages.name: Mixe–Zoque
mixe-zoque-languages.summary: A family of languages spoken around Mexico's Isthmus of Tehuantepec, including Mixe and Zoque, with roughly a dozen distinct languages recognized today.

terrence-kaufman.name: Terrence Kaufman
terrence-kaufman.summary: An American linguist (1937-2022) known for documenting Indigenous languages of Mexico and Central America and for work in Mesoamerican historical linguistics.

tzolk-in.name: Tzolkʼin
tzolk-in.summary: 260-day Mesoamerican calendar used by the Maya civilization, still kept by some Maya communities in the Guatemalan highlands today.

haab.name: Haabʼ
haab.summary: A 365-day calendar that formed part of the Maya calendric system, used by many pre-Columbian cultures of Mesoamerica.

maya-calendar.name: Calendar Round
maya-calendar.summary: A calendar system used across pre-Columbian Mesoamerica since at least the 5th century BC, shared with earlier cultures like the Olmec and Zapotec, and credited by Maya myth to the deity Itzamna.

guerrero.name: Guerrero
guerrero.summary: A mountainous Mexican state on the Pacific coast, home to Acapulco, named after independence leader and later president Vicente Guerrero.

nayarit.name: Nayarit
nayarit.summary: A Mexican Pacific coast state home to Uto-Aztecan peoples such as the Huichol and Cora, exposed to Spanish conquest in the 16th century with resistance lasting until 1722.

chichen-itza.name: Chichen Itza
chichen-itza.summary: A large Maya city in Yucatán, Mexico, that flourished from about 600 to 900 AD, blending Maya and central Mexican architectural styles, possibly reflecting a diverse population.

zapotec-script.name: Zapotec script
zapotec-script.summary: The earliest writing system of Mesoamerica's Zapotec culture, centered on Monte Albán in Oaxaca; despite many carved stone inscriptions, it remains largely undeciphered.

codex-chimalpopoca.name: Anales de Cuauhtitlan
codex-chimalpopoca.summary: Part of the postconquest Codex Chimalpopoca that records the pre-Hispanic history of Central Mexico.

c-catl-topiltzin.name: Ce Acatl Topiltzin
c-catl-topiltzin.summary: A mythologised 10th-century Toltec ruler in Aztec tradition, later a cultural hero often confused with the god Quetzalcoatl; legend credits the exiled Toltec Ce Acatl Topiltzin with founding Cuzcatlán in El Salvador.

vicente-riva-palacio.name: Vicente Riva Palacio
vicente-riva-palacio.summary: A 19th-century Mexican liberal politician, novelist and historian, grandson of independence hero Vicente Guerrero, who led forces against the French-backed empire of Maximilian I.

quetzalc-tl.name: Quetzalcoatl
quetzalc-tl.summary: A major Aztec deity, the 'Feathered Serpent', linked to wind, the planet Venus, the sun, learning and the priesthood; later accounts conflated him with a legendary Toltec ruler.

uxmal.name: Uxmal
uxmal.summary: An ancient Maya city of the classical period in Mexico's Puuc region, noted for its elaborate architecture and now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

nonoalca.name: Nonoalca
nonoalca.summary: A Mesoamerican people who played a major role in Toltec culture, forming most of the devotees of Quetzalcoatl at Tula and later scattering across the region.

tezcatlipoca.name: Tezcatlipoca
tezcatlipoca.summary: A central Aztec deity linked to the night sky, hurricanes, obsidian and conflict, one of four sons of the primordial dual deity; his main festival involved human sacrifice.

chichimeca.name: Chichimeca
chichimeca.summary: A term the Aztecs and Spanish used for nomadic and semi-nomadic peoples of north-central Mexico, comparable to "barbarian," who fiercely resisted Spanish expansion.

itza-people.name: Itza
itza-people.summary: A Maya ethnic group descended from the Chontal Chanes who settled around Lake Petén Itzá and remained independent there until conquered by the Spanish in 1697.

kukulkan.name: Kukulkan
kukulkan.summary: Feathered serpent deity of Maya mythology, worshipped at sites such as Chichen Itza, Uxmal and Mayapan.

put-n.name: Putún Maya
put-n.summary: A Mayan ethnic group from the Gulf Coast lowlands, generally synonymous with the Chontal Maya, considered more Mexicanized than their contemporaries and linked to the Itza.

xochicalco.name: Xochicalco
xochicalco.summary: A pre-Columbian archaeological site in Morelos, Mexico, that flourished after Teotihuacan's fall during the Epiclassic period (AD 700-900), reaching a population of up to 20,000.

cacaxtla.name: Cacaxtla
cacaxtla.summary: A Mexican archaeological site with a palace of vividly colored Maya-style murals, flourishing from about 650 to 900 CE.

cholula-mesoamerican-site.name: Cholula
cholula-mesoamerican-site.summary: A pre-Columbian Mesoamerican city near modern Puebla, Mexico, and a key religious center home to the largest pyramid structure by volume in the world.

great-goddess-of-teotihuacan.name: Great Goddess
great-goddess-of-teotihuacan.summary: A proposed deity of the pre-Columbian Teotihuacan civilization (about 100 BCE to 700 CE), thought to have ruled over the underworld, darkness, earth, water, war and possibly creation itself.

q-uq-umatz.name: Qʼuqʼumatz (Gukumatz)
q-uq-umatz.summary: A Feathered Serpent god of wind, rain and creation among the Postclassic Kʼicheʼ Maya, equivalent to the Aztec Quetzalcoatl and the Yucatec Maya's Kukulkan.

itzamna.name: Itzamna
itzamna.summary: A major creator deity in Maya mythology, an upper god believed to reside in the sky, called 'God D' by archaeologists before his name was deciphered.

leopoldo-batres.name: Leopoldo Batres
leopoldo-batres.summary: Mexican army officer turned pioneering archaeologist (1852-1926) who excavated at Teotihuacan, Monte Albán, Xochicalco and other sites and made Mexico's first archaeological maps, though his restoration work was sometimes flawed.

hun-hunahpu.name: Hun Hunahpu
hun-hunahpu.summary: A figure in Maya mythology from the Popol Vuh, father of the Hero Twins; tricked and sacrificed by the underworld lords, his severed head later impregnated a woman who bore the twins.

feathered-serpent.name: Feathered Serpent
feathered-serpent.summary: A supernatural deity found across Mesoamerican religions, known as Quetzalcōātl to the Aztecs and Kukulkan to the Maya, its feathers and serpent body symbolizing divine and earthly natures.

chaac.name: Chaac
chaac.summary: The Maya god of rain, thunder and lightning, who strikes clouds with a lightning axe to make them produce rain; he corresponds to the Aztec god Tlaloc.

pipil-people.name: Pipil
pipil-people.summary: An indigenous Mesoamerican people, a subgroup of the Nahua, who lived in what is now western and central El Salvador and Nicaragua and spoke the Nawat language.

ch-orti-people.name: Ch'orti' people
ch-orti-people.summary: An Indigenous Maya people living in Guatemala, Honduras and El Salvador, whose language descends from the Classic Maya of the Copán inscriptions.

oasisamerica.name: Oasisamerica
oasisamerica.summary: A cultural region of Indigenous peoples spanning parts of the southwestern United States and northwestern Mexico, whose precontact cultures were largely agrarian, unlike neighboring Aridoamerica.

aridoamerica.name: Aridoamerica
aridoamerica.summary: A dry cultural and ecological region across northern Mexico and the southwestern United States, distinguished from the more fertile Mesoamerica to its south.

soconusco.name: Soconusco
soconusco.summary: A fertile coastal region of southeastern Mexico near Guatemala, home to the early Mokaya and Olmec cultures, whose economy centred on cacao and rubber.
